seo_title: Jersey Devil: Pine Barrens legend and the 1909 panic
seo_desc: Where the Jersey Devil came from: Mother Leeds and the Leeds family, Benjamin Franklin's almanac feud, and the January 1909 panic that gave it wings.
summary: The Pine Barrens devil of southern New Jersey, with a stranger origin than the cursed-baby story and one very loud week in January 1909.
body: The Jersey Devil is the monster of the Pine Barrens, the pine and cedar swamp country of southern New Jersey. The description settles into the same shape every time, a horse or goat head, bat wings, clawed hands, hooves and a forked tail, and a scream that witnesses describe the same way.

The popular story has Mother Leeds cursing her thirteenth child in 1735 and the thing flying up the chimney. The less told story is that the name came out of colonial politics and a newspaper feud, and the creature only got its wings after a week of mass panic in 1909.
There is no killing that anyone can point to and no photograph that survives a second look. I love the legend. I just don't think there's an animal behind it.

sections.h: Mother Leeds and the thirteenth child
p: A woman named Leeds in the Pine Barrens already had twelve children. When she found out she was pregnant with a thirteenth she cursed it out loud and said let this one be the devil. The baby arrived looking normal, then grew wings, hooves, a tail and claws, thrashed the room with its tail and flew up the chimney into the pines.

Nobody agrees on the year or the place. 1735 at Leeds Point is the version you see most, though some tell it at Burlington and one version sets it near Mays Landing around 1855, where Mrs. Leeds wished for a devil instead of a baby and got one.

There was a real family. Deborah Leeds and her husband Japhet Leeds lived at Leeds Point, and Japhet's will from 1736 names twelve children, which lines up too neatly with the story to shrug off. Whether that's the seed of the legend or a coincidence is a fair question (I lean towards the family being the seed, for reasons below).

sections.h: The almanac war behind the name
p: Brian Regal, a historian of science at Kean University, went looking for the origin and came back with a colonial fight instead of a cursed baby, and his version explains why the creature ended up with bat wings.

Daniel Leeds was a surveyor and almanac publisher in colonial New Jersey who got sideways with the local Quakers by printing astrological material, which his congregation decided was pagan. They censored and destroyed his almanacs. He kept printing, converted to Anglicanism, wrote anti-Quaker tracts and sided with the royal governor, and in 1700 a Quaker pamphlet called Satan's Harbinger Encountered accused him in print of working for the devil.

His son Titan Leeds took over the almanac business, which put him up against Benjamin Franklin's Poor Richard's Almanack. In 1733 Franklin jokingly predicted in print that Titan Leeds would die that October, Leeds called him a fool and a liar in public, and Franklin answered by insisting Leeds really had died and that the almanacs coming out under his name must be the work of his ghost. He kept at it after Leeds actually died in 1738.

The Leeds family crest had a wyvern on it, a two-legged dragon with bat wings. Regal's argument is that a family the neighbours already saw as religious and political outcasts, with a dragon on the letterhead and a public feud with Franklin running, turned into the Leeds Devil in local gossip. The name shows up in print as Leeds Devil or Devil of Leeds long before anyone writes Jersey Devil.

For the week of January 16 to 23, 1909, newspapers across South Jersey and Philadelphia ran hundreds of reports. It seems to have started with strange tracks in the snow and then snowballed, because people were soon seeing the thing itself across South Jersey and as far off as Delaware and western Maryland.

The reports from that week are the good part. The creature attacked a trolley car in Haddon Heights, turned up at a social club in Camden, and police in Camden and Bristol, Pennsylvania supposedly fired at it and hit nothing. Schools closed, workers stayed home, and armed groups went into the pines to hunt it.

The Philadelphia Zoo reportedly offered $10,000, which brought out the hoaxers, including a kangaroo fitted with fake claws and bat wings (a kangaroo with fake bat wings, which is the finest piece of work this country has ever produced). That's the level of craft the Jersey Devil inspired in 1909.

Once a legend gets going, big names attach themselves. Joseph Bonaparte, Napoleon's older brother, is said to have seen the Jersey Devil while hunting on his estate at Bordentown around 1820. Commodore Stephen Decatur supposedly saw a flying creature at the Hanover Mill Works, fired a cannonball at it and missed. Neither story comes with anything you'd call evidence.

Other bits of the record are more ordinary. Livestock killings blamed on the devil in 1840, more in 1841 with tracks and screams, a Greenwich Township farmer in 1925 who shot something going after his chickens and photographed the body, and a red-eyed animal in Downingtown, Pennsylvania in 1937 that a reporter compared to the Jersey Devil. In 1960 the merchants around Camden offered $10,000 for capture and said they'd build a zoo for it. Nobody produced the animal.

The name also travelled further than the pines ever did. When the NHL's Colorado Rockies moved east in 1982 the franchise became the New Jersey Devils, so the state's hockey team is named after a monster that may have started as an insult about a surveyor's family (the most profitable thing the creature has ever done).

Most of the explaining is about people. The Pine Barrens were the kind of place outsiders were told to stay out of, full of pine robbers, deserters and families living outside the rules, and a reputation for monsters kept strangers away. Two eugenics studies from the early 20th century made it worse by describing Barrens residents as criminals and defectives, research that is now considered biased, unscientific and probably falsified.

Misidentified animals finish the job. A great horned owl crossing a road, a heron taking off, a deer breaking cover, and the scream of a fox or a screech owl that sounds like a woman in trouble. Once the 1909 papers had printed a winged horse-headed devil, every strange thing in those woods got fitted to it.

If you want the ground itself, Leeds Point in Atlantic County is where the story is anchored, with a small monument and a general store that leans into it, and the pines run over a million acres from there. Batsto Village and Wharton State Forest are the easy way in. Go in daylight and pay attention to the roads, because the pines are flat and look the same in every direction and people get turned around out there every year.

faq.q: Where is the Jersey Devil located?
faq.a: The Pine Barrens of southern New Jersey, mainly around Leeds Point in Atlantic County and the forests of Burlington, Camden and Ocean counties. The 1909 reports spread across South Jersey, Philadelphia, Delaware and western Maryland, so people have seen it well outside the pines.

There's no animal. No remains have ever been found, and the photos don't hold up. Historians think the name started with the Leeds family and colonial politics, and the familiar winged description was fixed by a week of newspaper panic in 1909. The sightings were real enough in that people made them.

faq.q: Where did the Mother Leeds story come from?
faq.a: There was a real Leeds family at Leeds Point, and Japhet Leeds's 1736 will names twelve children, which fits a story about a thirteenth. Historian Brian Regal argues the devil reputation grew out of the family's quarrels with local Quakers, a pamphlet accusing Daniel Leeds of working for the devil, and Benjamin Franklin treating his son Titan Leeds as a ghost in their almanac feud.

faq.q: Did schools really close during the Jersey Devil panic?
faq.a: Several did during the week of January 16 to 23, 1909, and some mills and businesses let workers stay home. Armed groups went into the pines after it. The Philadelphia Zoo's $10,000 reward is usually reported as an offer made at the time, and it brought out hoaxes, including a kangaroo with fake wings.

faq.q: Why is the New Jersey hockey team called the Devils?
faq.a: The franchise moved from Colorado in 1982 and took the name New Jersey Devils from the Pine Barrens legend. It's been better for the team than it ever was for the monster.
